============================================================
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN
============================================================

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
------------------------------------------------------------------
Preferred strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DiD) with provider- and year-fixed effects, complemented by an event-study.

Why it fits:
•  The report-card policy arrives at a clearly observed date and applies to every provider in one region (“treated”).  
•  We can construct an otherwise comparable set of providers located in regions that did not adopt report cards during the sample window (“controls”).  
•  With multiple pre- and post-policy years, a DiD specification recovers the average treatment-on-the-treated (ATT) under the parallel-trends assumption.  
•  Provider and calendar-year fixed effects absorb (i) all time-invariant provider heterogeneity and (ii) shocks common to all providers in a given year.  
•  The event-study variant lets us (a) test for pre-trends, (b) visualise dynamic responses, and (c) observe whether effects grow or fade.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
    Treat_i = 1 if provider i operates in the region in which report cards become publicly available; 0 otherwise.

Treatment timing  
    Post_t = 1 for calendar years t ≥ τ*, where τ* is the first year report cards are released.

Main interaction  
    Treat_i × Post_t  (the DiD term)

Control group (counterfactual)  
    Providers in neighbouring / otherwise similar regions that do **not** release report cards during the observation window.  
    •  Match on hospital type (acute-care, specialty), size, teaching status, baseline quality, and patient mix.  
    •  Exclude border-zone providers in robustness checks to minimise spillovers.

Outcomes  
    •  Performance metrics: risk-adjusted mortality, readmission rate, surgical complication index, average LOS.  
    •  Patient outcomes: 30-day survival, functional-status improvement, patient-satisfaction scores.  
    •  Input adjustments: staffing ratios, high-tech capital, case-mix severity.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends – In absence of the policy, the evolution of outcomes for treated and control providers would have followed the same trend.  
      Plausibility: We have several pre-periods; regions are chosen to be socio-demographically similar; pre-trend tests will be performed.

A2. No spillovers/contamination – Report cards in Region T do not directly affect providers or patients in Region C.  
      Plausibility: Geographic distance and separate media markets limit cross-region viewership; border providers will be excluded in a robustness check.

A3. Stable composition – Entry/exit or mergers are not systematically induced by the policy in a way correlated with potential outcomes.  
      Plausibility: Entry barriers in health care are high; we will keep a balanced panel and test robustness to dropping entrants/exits.

A4. Measurement consistency – Definition and coding of performance/outcome variables remain unchanged over time and across regions.  
      Plausibility: Data come from the same administrative source with uniform coding standards.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION
------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends / hidden shocks (e.g., concurrent quality-improvement program only in treated region).  
    •  Mitigation: Event-study to inspect and formally test for pre-trends. Add region-specific time trends. Control for observable concurrent policies.

T2. Patient sorting in response to report cards (better patients flock to high-rated hospitals, worsening case-mix at low-rated ones).  
    •  Mitigation: Use risk-adjusted outcomes; include patient-level controls aggregated to provider-year; instrument patient volumes in a separate 2SLS robustness (distance-based instrument).

T3. Provider attrition or coding manipulation post-policy.  
    •  Mitigation: Balanced-panel core sample; robustness dropping providers with large coding jumps; Benford or McCrary density tests on diagnosis coding.

5. R CODE OUTLINE
------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
# ------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # high-performance fixed-effects regressions
library(ggplot2)      # visuals

# ------------------------------------------
# 1.  Data loading
# ------------------------------------------
# Assume two CSVs: providers.csv (panel) and region_lookup.csv
prov <- fread("providers.csv")          # provider-year panel
region <- fread("region_lookup.csv")    # provider_id | region | treat_region

# ------------------------------------------
# 2.  Merge & variable construction
# ------------------------------------------
d <- merge(prov, region, by = "provider_id")

# treatment dummy
d[, treat := as.integer(treat_region == 1)]

# policy implementation year in treated region
policy_year <- 2016  # example; replace with actual

# post dummy
d[, post := as.integer(year >= policy_year)]

# interaction
d[, treat_post := treat * post]

# risk-adjusted mortality already in data as `risk_adj_mort`
# add provider & year factors (fixest handles internally)

# ------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main DiD regression
# ------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(risk_adj_mort ~ treat_post + covariate1 + covariate2 |
                  provider_id + year,
                  data = d, cluster = "region")

summary(did_main)

# ------------------------------------------
# 4.  Event-study (dynamic effects)
# ------------------------------------------
d[, rel_year := year - policy_year]                # event time
d[, event_d := interaction(treat, rel_year)]       # fixest helper

event <- feols(risk_adj_mort ~ i(rel_year, treat) + covariate1 + covariate2 |
               provider_id + year,
               data = d[rel_year %between% c(-5,5)], cluster = "region")

iplot(event)   # fixest built-in plot of dynamic effects

# ------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness: Exclude border providers
# ------------------------------------------
d_rb <- d[border_provider == 0]  # binary indicator
did_rb <- feols(risk_adj_mort ~ treat_post + covariate1 + covariate2 |
                provider_id + year,
                data = d_rb, cluster = "region")
summary(did_rb)
```

Key notes:
•  `covariate1`, `covariate2` placeholders stand for time-varying controls (case-mix index, bed count, teaching status changes, etc.).  
•  `cluster = "region"` allows for arbitrary serial correlation within regions. If region count < 40, use wild-cluster bootstrap.

6. EXPECTED RESULTS
------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition: Public disclosure raises reputational stakes and introduces market-like incentives. Low-performing providers improve or lose patients; high-performers may have less scope for gain.

Direction:  
    •  Average treated provider: Risk-adjusted mortality ↓, readmissions ↓, patient-satisfaction ↑.  
Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope):  
    •  1–2 percentage-point drop in 30-day mortality (baseline ≈ 10 %).  
    •  3–5 % decline in readmissions.  
    •  Modest increase (0.1–0.2 SD) in patient-experience scores.  
These are in line with earlier transparency interventions (e.g., cardiac surgery report cards).

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT
------------------------------------------------------------------
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0.5 = partly, 0 = doubtful)

1. Parallel trends supported by pre-policy data ............... 0.8  
2. No spillovers / SUTVA ...................................... 0.7  
3. No simultaneity / reverse causality ........................ 0.9  
4. Measurement consistency across regions/time ................ 0.9  
5. Robust standard errors & inference ......................... 1.0  
Overall average score: 0.86  → Reasonably strong design, but vigilance required on spillovers and pre-trend diagnostics.

============================================================
